title: Ocular Stroke: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO)
summary: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) is a true ocular emergency characterized by sudden, painless monocular vision loss. It represents the ocular equivalent of a cerebral stroke and requires immediate neuro-ophthalmic triage.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: CRAO is an infarction of the inner retinal layers due to blockage of the central retinal artery. The central retinal artery is an end-artery, meaning there is no collateral circulation. Retinal viability is lost after approximately 90-100 minutes of total occlusion.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Fundoscopy
content: Sudden, profound painless loss of vision (typically 'counting fingers' or 'hand motion').
Fundoscopy: 'Cherry-red spot' at the fovea (due to choroidal blood supply).
Retinal whitening: Edematous, necrotic inner retina.
Cattle-trucking (segmentation of blood flow in arterioles).

rows: Scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP elevation

sections.title: Emergency Protocols
content: Rule out Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with STAT ESR, CRP, and Platelet count.
Immediate stroke workup (Carotid Doppler, EKG, Echo, MRI Brain) is mandatory.
Irreversible retinal damage occurs after 90-100 minutes of occlusion.
Rule out hypercoagulable states in patients under 50 years of age.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Ocular massage (digital pressure to induce movement of embolus).
Step 2: Lower Intraocular Pressure (Topical timolol, acetazolamide 500mg IV).
Step 3: Paracentesis (if within 2-4 hours, though efficacy is debated).
Step 4: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (if available within 8-24 hours).
Step 5: Systemic anticoagulation/thrombolytics (if indicated by neuro-consult).

content.explanation: S: Sudden vision loss, T: Thinning of vessels, O: Ocular massage, K: Kidney function check (for contrast), E: ESR/CRP for GCA.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls
content: Cilioretinal artery sparing: Occurs in 15-30% of eyes, preserving central visual acuity.
Prognosis is generally poor; no randomized trial has proven superiority of a single treatment.
